#6687. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6685. Mary Lovelace O’Neal Broke the Rules of Black Art

Marianne Boesky in New York mounts the late abstract artist’s first posthumous show, “Requiem”

Mary Lovelace O’Neal moved to New York in the late 1960s at the height of the Black Arts movement. The Mississippi-born artist enrolled at Columbia’s School of the Arts in 1968, where she honed her distinct take on Abstract Expressionist painting. Blazing a trail as one of the few Black women in this field, she faced criticism from her peers, who felt her work should engage more directly with the political issues of the time, that it was not “Black enough.” She responded with her so-called “lampblack” paintings; radical, pitch-black abstractions made with carbon soot, allowing her to retain her expressionistic sensibility while answering the social question of Black art.

But this response to socially conscious art through Minimalism never fully defined her career. Lovelace O’Neal relocated to San Francisco after graduating from Columbia, where she reignited her exploration of color and abstraction. Her black color fields “unzipped,” as she called it, to reveal new, kaleidoscopic abstractions. By the 1980s and through the ’90s, O’Neal developed her idiosyncratic expressionistic style, often meditating on tangible subjects through obscure, gestural paintings. Requiem for a Daffodil (1997), a six-by-11-foot painting, embodies this bold, high-energy approach. It features floral forms, from yellow bouquets to a field of delicate white flowers running across the top border, gathered together for what can only be understood as a funeral. Lovelace O’Neal’s vigorous brushstrokes streak across the canvas, yet the work retains a sensitivity, a delicate and caring touch for the subjects that populated her abstract works. It is perhaps the best representation of the middle part of her six-decade career. These two decades are the subject of the appropriately titled “Requiem,” at New York’s Marianne Boesky Gallery, her first posthumous show on view through December 19.

“The painting, Requiem for a Daffodil, to me, is an expression of the depth to which Mary could feel for her subjects,” gallerist Marianne Boesky tells Bazaar. “A funeral dedicated to a flower, attended by flowers, delivered with such solemnity, is a reflection of Mary’s acceptance and understanding of the loss of something beautiful, innocent, fleeting.”

Lovelace O’Neal died on May 10 at her home in Mérida, Mexico, at 84. Born in Mississippi and raised in Arkansas, she left home in 1960 to study under David Driskell at Howard University in Washington, D.C., before briefly attending Maine’s Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture in 1963. At this school, she devoted herself to Abstract Expressionism, studying the work of Franz Kline and Willem de Kooning.

Lovelace O'Neal lived what can only be called an exciting life, documented through archival material in the back room of Boesky Gallery. While living in California, she also traveled the world, collecting memories and experiences on jaunts from South America to Africa that informed her paintings. Panthers with Socks (1985–90) epitomized this process; the frenetic abstraction of a leaping white cat draws on both her twenties in New York and her 1984 trip to Morocco.

“In Panthers with Socks, the brushy figure of this leaping animal makes for a clear allusion to the Black Panther Party and the artist’s involvement in the Civil Rights Movement,” Boesky explains. “While the sights, sounds, and memories of the artist’s time in Morocco inspire the bold colors and theatrical architecture of the composition.”

Although Lovelace O’Neal leaned away from overt political work during the 1960s, her abstract painting never abandoned concerns about race and notions of Blackness. One example in the show, Juke Joint (1997), referenced the Jim Crow-era establishments where Black communities gathered, places Mary witnessed firsthand growing up in the Southern United States. The gestural work conveys the movement of dancing legs, evoking the free spirit of these establishments.

The eighties and nineties were largely defined by her life as a teacher. The artist joined the Department of Art Practice at the University of California, Berkeley, as a professor in the ’70s and received tenure in 1985. “I wanted to pay tribute to her as both an epic painter and as a lifelong teacher,” Boesky says. To do so, the gallerist intentionally paired Lovelace O’Neal’s show with Michaela Yearwood-Dan, a 32-year-old Black Abstract painter, who opened her solo show, “A Woman of Will,” the same night.

“[When I first saw Mary’s paintings,] it was really the first time I felt like I had really come across a female Black abstract painter who felt uncontained,” Yearwood-Dan tells Bazaar. “There was a real sense of freedom, lack of control. but in an intentional, free-spirited way.”

By juxtaposing these two shows, Boesky facilitates a cross-generational dialogue between the two artists, who, despite admiring one another’s work, never met in person. “Mary admired the energy and color in Michaela’s abstract paintings and quickly grasped Michaela’s commitment to activism, which also underpinned her paintings,” Boesky says. “Michaela had known about and followed Mary’s work, unbeknownst to me, at the time I began working with both of them. Completely different generations and geographies but kindred spirits nonetheless. It felt like kismet to present their shows side by side.”

That the work still resonates across generations underscores Lovelace O’Neal’s lasting power. The paintings on view at Boesky reveal how the artist used abstraction to layer unmitigated expression and feeling into her subjects, from people and animals to place and memory. “She understood early that ideas and emotions had the potential to be conveyed more powerfully through abstraction than through identifiable narration,” Boesky says. Viewers can catch glimpses of a pig in What’s time to a pig (c. 1990s), or potted plants in A Tree Branch (c. 1990-91) amid the frenzied mark-making. Boesky says these images “stampede across a canvas or hover like a dream.”

Lovelace O’Neal offers a sneak peek into her dreams—her mind—through these paintings. The beauty of “Requiem” is that it compiles works from the undeniable turning point of her career. The works still feature the lampblack foundation, while also capturing how color furiously reemerged in her practice. Seen for the first time since her passing, the work remains as potent as ever, a product of a life devoted to her idiosyncratic vision.

“She referred to the act of painting as labor, her life’s labor,” Boesky says. “And she referred to the paintings as her children, the product of that labor, put out into the world to make their own mischief.”

#6684. Haven and Converse Made One of the Coolest Chucks of the Year

As perfect as the Converse Chuck Taylor is, that hasn’t stopped the OG sneaker brand from pushing the sneaker's limits through countless collaborations that remake the classic Chucks in a million different images. While most of those collabs tend to be flashier, there are a few that stand out for their restraint. Or at least, what appears to be restraint at first glance. After a sellout partnership, Canadian outfitters and tastemakers Haven have reunited with Converse for its second team-up, lifting the vaunted Chuck 70 to new heights.

Haven’s disciplined approach to design considers its roots in Vancouver, the topography and climes therein, and incorporates that into its garments. Think waterproof shells, lightweight insulation, gussets for range of motion. “We think about the real world. What do you actually need to wear and what do you need to make you comfortable, and how to make your day a little bit better,” Haven cofounder Arthur Chmielewski says. “It could be just 1 per cent better. But those little details over time, they make your life a little bit better, right?” But it’s not just optimizing in the most sterile sense. Chmielewski also goes to great lengths to consider both comfort and craft in every product, employing details like Japanese denim and Loro Piana cashmere into the brand’s range. So when it comes to tackling an established iconic product, how does Haven do it?

“If you were to think of a farm-to-table kind of approach, it's like using the best ingredients to make the best food. And we're always thinking about that approach as well from a product standpoint,” Chmielewski says. The sneakers are all about subtle details that sum up to a better experience of something that was already pretty great to begin with. A tonal color palette combines different textures of leather, cashmere suede and hairy suede, giving each pair tactile depth that only becomes more pronounced with wear. The Chuck Taylor’s signature rubber toe cap is also replaced with a natural white leather toe cap, a detail that would go undetected more than five feet away. Practically, Haven’s also added an easy-access side-zip made from high-quality custom YKK Excella zippers as well as an additional rubber sole for longevity.

The full magnitude of the sneaker’s design is left for the wearer to experience. Details like reinforced vamps and eyestays, soft leather lining, and an upgraded Ortholite cushioned insole make the shoes more than just pretty to look at.

”The crew at Haven are just so good at translating their signature aesthetic across all products they touch,” says Matt Sleep, Design Lead for Converse Energy. “You see the shoes and instantly you know it fits into their aesthetic ecosystem. You just know it’s Haven without needing to see a logo wildly emblazoned anywhere.”

For a modern label rooted in the classics, the Chuck Taylor is a fitting project. Because, for Chmielewski, it’s all about making things that will last a long time. From the components to the iconic silhouette, you can bet you’ll see a pair of these knocking around for years to come.

#6683. The Great Bear Rainforest: How Fashion Rallied to Stop the Deforestation of an Ancient Rainforest

This story is part of ‘The Business Case for Nature’, a series exploring fashion’s impact on nature and vice versa. Read more here.

The Great Bear Rainforest, spanning 6.4 million hectares from the Alaskan border to just above Vancouver Island, is the largest coastal temperate rainforest in the world, a critical carbon sink, and the only known home of the extremely rare white-furred spirit bear. Whales migrate through the rainforest year-round, and it is a major breeding ground for all five species of Pacific salmon. Thanks to the region’s heavy rainfall and nutrient-rich ecosystem, it also houses an array of ancient trees over a thousand years old, including sitka spruce (among the tallest trees in the world) and red western cedar (which hold deep cultural significance for the 26 local First Nations).

Until 2016, 90% of the Great Bear Rainforest was open for logging, and fashion was one of the industries profiting from it. The industry uses large quantities of man-made cellulosic fibers (MMCF) like viscose, modal and lyocell, which typically come from wood pulp. It also has a direct link to deforestation through wood-based packaging, and an indirect link through leather and cotton, which are often grown on deforested land.

Now, thanks to fashion brands joining anti-logging campaigners at a crucial moment, 85% of it is legally protected from deforestation and logging, the First Nations whose territories overlap with it are co-decision makers in its conservation, and there is a $120 million fund helping them transition to conservation-based economies. This is a rare example of fashion rallying around nature restoration and using its purchasing power for good, in partnership with other industries. Experts say it’s a blueprint the industry could apply elsewhere.

This “seismic” win took decades to achieve, says Nicole Rycroft, founder and executive director of non-profit Canopy, which works to conserve ancient and endangered forests around the world. While anti-logging efforts in the Great Bear Rainforest pre-date Canopy, the non-profit joined the campaign at a critical junction, leveraging fashion industry partners including H&M and Zara, to secure the groundbreaking land use agreement when momentum was slowing. “Canopy was one of several organizations that started working with international corporate customers of forest products coming out of that region to send a very clear signal that we don’t want to be sourcing from clear cuts of massive, ecologically critical, temperate rainforests, and we don’t want to be sourcing from spirit bear habitat,” she explains.

A decade on, Vogue Business invited Rycroft to reflect on what the Great Bear Rainforest can teach fashion about nature conservation, and using its purchasing power for good.

Logging happens at the beginning of the supply chain, several steps upstream from where brand traceability programs tend to stop. With such a complex, sprawling supply chain, and such a small number of brands on the hook to comply with traceability regulations, few brands have visibility beyond Tier 1 (garment manufacturing) or Tier 2 (fabric production). Logging would come under Tier 4. That’s why meaningful action starts with traceability, says Rycroft, so brands can understand where their deforestation risks are.

But brands don’t need a direct link to deforestation to make a difference in conservation campaigns. “Even if it’s not a direct or immediate sourcing link, the adjacency is really relevant,” says Rycroft. “Brands are still seen as important even if they’re not existing customers, because there is the potential for them to be future customers.”

Anti-logging efforts in the Great Bear Rainforest started in earnest in the mid-1990s, with conservation organizations standing shoulder to shoulder with local First Nations. But the forestry industry was powerful, so media coverage was largely limited to British Columbia, framing the conflict as a domestic “war in the woods” and failing to break through on the international stage. The turning point came when international brands began sending clear signals to the forestry industry that they did not want to source from ancient and endangered ecosystems. This included home improvement companies such as Home Depot and Lowe’s, as well as major retailers like Sainsbury’s.

But even after the various parties agreed to work toward a land use agreement, progress ebbed and flowed. It took more than a decade to reach a legal agreement, during which time brands and conservations continually applied pressure to keep negotiations on track. “It took consumer companies making phone calls and writing letters to individual forestry companies,” says Rycroft. Fashion joined in later. “The process was long and arduous, and for a long time, there was a blindspot around fashion’s footprint in the Great Bear Rainforest.”

It was Canopy that rallied the fashion industry to get involved. In 2013, it created Canopy Style, an initiative where leading fashion brands commit to end sourcing from ancient and endangered forests. One of the early adopters was Stella McCartney. Within a few months of signing onto the pledge, McCartney canceled her contract with a dissolving pulp mill on Vancouver Island, which was sourcing directly from the Great Bear Rainforest, Canopy discovered. “It sent a very clear signal that fashion is a force to be reckoned with,” says Rycroft.

Later down the line, around 2016, progress stalled again. The land use agreement was 18 months overdue, and even the most ardent supporters were starting to feel stuck. Canopy teamed up with national newspaper The Globe and Mail to host a customer-investor roundtable. The date was set for a month ahead. They invited leading politicians, the forest industry and the First Nations leaders that had been involved in the negotiating process, as well as conservation partners and 70 people representing 70 international brands, including Stella McCartney, Eileen Fisher, H&M, and Zara. “Within days of issuing the invitation, the spirit and intent at the negotiating table changed,” says Rycroft. Twenty-four hours before the roundtable was due to take place, the British Columbia government announced the draft land use agreement.

“Brands have incredible social capital and influence, in addition to being an important economic sector,” says Rycroft. “They can’t be afraid to lean in and flex that muscle.”

Brands that sign up to Canopy Style — or Canopy’s equivalent packaging initiative, Pack4Good — commit to stop sourcing from ancient and endangered forests. That’s the baseline, says Rycroft, the Great Bear Rainforest case study shows that fashion’s nature strategies need to go one step further. They also need to include scaling next-gen and circular alternatives that can ease the industry’s burden on nature, and the risk that burden poses to supply chain resilience.

“Next-gen and circular alternatives are the off-ramp from deforestation and forest degradation,” explains Rycroft. “Brands will not be able to eliminate — or even substantially mitigate — their risk of sourcing from high-carbon, high-biodiversity forests unless we have scaled alternatives.”

At last month’s Textile Exchange conference, Canopy walked the industry through Next Gen Warp Speed, its new initiative that makes the business case for brands to convert 5% of their MMCF basket to next-gen alternatives by 2028. Fashion’s struggle to scale next-gen materials has been well-documented, but Canopy is hoping that a 5% commitment is enough to tip the balance without putting a substantial burden on brands to fund the transition. “A big focus for us now is: how do we create the right conditions and pre-competitive vehicles to scale next-gen production?” says Rycroft.

Moving forward, Canopy is applying its learnings from the Great Bear Rainforest win to other critical ecosystems around the world. Top of its list are the Amazon rainforest and the Leuser Ecosystem in Indonesia, where it already has brand buy-in from the likes of Eileen Fisher and Stella McCartney. Rycroft says she is hopeful that fashion can make a significant difference in these landscapes, just as it did in British Columbia.

A few weeks ago, Rycroft traveled up to the Great Bear Rainforest to see the ecosystem Canopy had worked for so many years to protect. She sat on a riverbank and watched a spirit bear pick salmon out of the stream. “So many people dedicated their lives to this cause, or made a call at a critical juncture, to enable that to happen. It has made such a dramatic difference to the landscape. And now the Great Bear Rainforest truly is a landscape of hope.”

#6682. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6680. Ana de Armas’s Complete Dating History

From Ben Affleck to Tom Cruise and beyond.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Ana de Armas has experienced a stratospheric rise in Hollywood over the past decade. 2015’s Knock Knock—a thriller starring Keanu Reeves—provided the Cuban, American, and Spanish actress with her stateside breakout role. Since then, de Armas has appeared in numerous box office and critical hits, such as 2017’s Blade Runner 2049, 2019’s Knives Out, 2021’s No Time to Die, 2022’s Blonde, and 2025’s John Wick spin-off Ballerina.

Offscreen, the actress has had several public romances, too. Most recently, she has been linked to Venezuelan singer Beto Montenegro, with the pair photographed kissing during a summer getaway in Spain. In November 2026, they made their first red carpet appearance together at the Latin Recording Academy’s Person of the Year Gala in Las Vegas.

Here’s what you need to know about Ana de Armas’s dating history.

Prior to making it big as a Hollywood actress, de Armas relocated from Havana to Spain, where she met her first husband, Marc Clotet. The Ghosted star began dating the Spanish model and actor in 2010, with the pair marrying the following year in July 2011, Hola! magazine reported.

Unfortunately, the couple’s marriage didn’t last. During an appearance at the 27th Goya Awards in Spain on Feb. 17, 2013, Clotet revealed, “Yes, we’ve broken up. It was by mutual agreement. The actress wore a black Wiederhoeft look featuring a corseted top and sheer lace skirt, while Montenegro opted for a black suit with a light blue shirt and dark tie.

#6679. Get to Know the Watchmaker Behind John Mayer’s Latest Pick-Up

When looking for the next big thing in the watch world, there are few better places to check than John Mayer’s wrist. The super collector can make his own Audemars Piguet Royal Oaks, skyrocket the value of a previously underappreciated Rolex Daytona, and help establish new indies. This week, Mayer is co-signing a hyper-limited-edition piece from FVF Genève, a watchmaker you should get to know.

FVF Genève is the brainchild of Spanish-born, Geneva-based watchmaker Franc Vila. Mayer is wearing his latest release: FVF2 Time & Day “Happy Monday,” made in partnership with American watch and jewelry retailer Material Good. On his Instagram, Mayer referred to the collaborators as a “Trifecta of Greatness.” There’s more to this piece than its mesmerizing mother-of-pearl, though. The watch’s design celebrates the idea that, if you love what you do, Monday mornings are actually something to look forward to.

The “Happy Monday” is a limited edition of seven pieces, each of which is engraved with a different day of the week on its rotor. The design is a reminder, as the brand says, that “each day is an opportunity to embrace our calling.” It helps, of course, that this message is delivered by a truly beautiful movement with black-polished surfaces, plenty of beveling and polishing, and great typography. Then there’s the rad day-of-the-week indicator on the dial. Situated between 6 and 9 o’clock, it takes the shape of a subtle gold track with a letter for each day of the week in French. To go with the “Happy Monday” theme, “Lundi” (Monday in French) is the only day represented by a standout green letter.

The dial is the showstopping element on this piece. It’s executed in a sparkly deep-blue mother-of-pearl and accented with thick gold-tone printing in the form of an outer minute track, a sub-seconds display between 4 and 5 o’clock, and bisecting lines that create a classically inspired “sector” design. The interplay of the sector when combined with mother-of-pearl is unusual enough, but add in the retrograde day-of-the-week indicator, and you’ve got a truly compelling combo.

The watch’s 39.5mm case is made out of Grade 5 titanium and features a Titalyt treatment—an electrochemical surface treatment that creates a ceramic-like layer and increases durability and hardness. F.P. Journe is a big fan of this treatment, and FVF uses it to great effect here. The finishing gives the Happy Monday a dark, industrial aesthetic that plays off the mother-of-pearl and gold tones on the dial for a distinctive feel. The watch comes on a matching beads-of-rice bracelet with straight endlinks, further adding to the interplay between vintage and modern inspiration. Finally, the crown and date corrector are located on the left side of the case rather than the right, where they typically sit.

Limited to just seven pieces—not including a unique piece that went to Material Good’s Yoni Ben-Yehuda—the $125,000 Happy Monday is the latest independent watch to receive a co-sign from super-collector John Mayer. Despite his role as Audemars Piguet's “Creative Conduit," Mayer has been known to support high-end independent makers such as F.P. Journe, and famously helped propel Vanguart onto the horological stage over the past year.

Vila, who established his eponymous luxury watch brand in the early 2000s, is a prime candidate to receive his flowers from the modern collecting community: marrying avant-garde case and dial designs with high complications. Vila sold his initial brand in the late 2000s, but he’s now having another go at creating modern classics with FVF. He’s come at the right time. It’s boom times for independent watchmakers as collectors try to identify the next big thing, and a co-sign from Mayer makes FVF a strong candidate to catch fire.

#6678. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

#6675. My Friend Joe Vanella Is a Traitor

I have known Joseph Vanella for multiple decades. The world has known him for about nine weeks, ever since he showed up on the latest season of The Traitors: New Blood as one of the civilians airdropped into a Scottish castle so they can be barked at by a feather-clad Alan Cummings while trying to determine who amongst the group are actively “murdering” the others. Vanella, as it turns out, is one of the murderers, and spends his time lying to almost everyone around him, feigning innocence in between doing ren faire cosplay in a turret with the two other traitors. He’s also on the ropes: this week’s episodes has the walls closing in, as one player (the dreaded Victor) convinces the group that Joe is…well, what he actually is, a Traitor. [Update: Joe got voted off. We’ve texted about it. He’s a champ.]

Joe Vanella—his actual last name, not at all made up!—is a Sopranos character come to life: big laugh, big body, big heart, proudly hails from Long Island, calls it “prazhoot” instead of prosciutto. He’s a family man (a wife, three small cute kids) and a funeral director (a job that runs in the family), and if you have a couple drinks with him, he will share stories about some truly absurd funerals he’s directed. Unlike many of his Traitors costars, he was not some form of influencer prior to getting cast.

He’s also now the subject of, like, three or four Traitors memes. People dressed as him for Halloween! And so I’ve spent a significant amount of time lately watching Joe, my friend, a guy I love, who texts the groupchat about gastronintestinal distress (tbh, we all do), also become a kind of breakout reality star. And not to make his newfound fame about me, but I wanted to know what’s going on with a guy who’s achieved that specific level of renown best described as A Guy.

So we talked about that—on zoom, with two kind NBC chaperones to make sure, I assume, Joe didn’t share any spoilers. We talked about how his wife feels about him being very good at lying. Being recognized at funerals he’s overseeing. And his now-complicated relationship with apples (Traitors fans will know).

GQ: Joseph Vanella, it’s great to meet you.

Vanella: Jon, thanks for being on time, buddy. That helped me out a lot.

I’m sorry I’m five minutes late. I’ve got a lot of meetings going on. I’m a very busy person, but not as popular as you.

Are we going to talk about how I beat your ass in fantasy baseball every year? Do we get to touch on that?

We absolutely will. But first, Joseph Vanella—Joey, as I know you; Joe, to the rest of the world now that you’re on Traitors—why did you go out for Traitors? Because we’ve never actually gotten into this, and I find it fascinating. A lot of people that I know, who also know you, have asked me, “Wait, why is Joe on Traitors?”

Okay. So we’ll start at the beginning. My wife, Meg, and I were looking for a show to watch, and my sister-in-law is like, "You guys got to watch Traitors." And it was after the first season. And we put it off, and then we watched it, and I immediately fell in love. We went through, I think, the first season in two days. We got into the second season. It sort of became a routine in our house. Every Thursday, I’d go to Carvel, get two sundaes. After the kids went to bed, we’d sit in there, we’d watch the new episode of Traitors. So, completely enamored with the show. There’s a casting call after season four, the Rob Rausch season. And Alan’s on TV, and he’s like, "We’re going to let regular people into the castle."

My sister-in-law, Erin, is going, "You got to do it. You got to do it." I’m like, "Ah, I don’t know." I haven’t been to the gym since my oldest kid was born. I’m like, this is the fattest I’ve been. Do I really want to be on TV? But I had a day at work, and afterward I made a video—and next thing I knew I was on a plane to Scotland. It was crazy. And also, as you saw how fat I am at this point in my life, it’s a show where I feel like I could get away without the athletic prowess needed for most other shows. So that was a positive, too.

Yeah, we’ll discuss your cardio at a later point in this interview. I do have to ask, did you go into this trying to get famous? Are you hoping to be famous? Do you want fame?

No. I went into this just to... You want to know the truth?

I went into this because I wanted to see the castle, I wanted to meet Alan, and I wanted to be on my favorite show. It’s the equivalent, at this point in my life, if you pick me up when I was 13 and drop me in The Simpsons, this is what this is to 44-year-old Joe Vanella. It’s picking me up and dropping me into my favorite show. And how many people get that opportunity?

Only 20-something people per season it looks like, and some didn’t make it very far, though you’ve made it pretty far. You did skip over a moment that I got to be part of, as you were in the process of possibly joining Traitors, where you were trying to figure out what to wear for a particular casting interview. And I’d like to revisit that moment because this is GQ, and so it’s apropos: at one point you texted me, midday, freaking out about needing to wear something to show yourself off properly. And what you texted me were a series of pants folded up into thirds, so I had no clue what they looked like. And then you also sent me some Vans that had tombstones on them, that you said you’d never worn.

They were caskets. They weren’t tombstones.

A pair of pants I was asked to assess as interview-worthy.

Sorry. Caskets. And I guess I wondered, what did you end up wearing that sealed the deal on your opportunity at Traitors? And did the casket Vans ever actually see the light of day? Will we see them on the Traitors?

The casket Vans sadly are still in a box up in my closet. I have not gotten to take them out yet. That particular interview, I wore a black shirt with pink flamingos on it.

A black button down shirt, pink flamingos. And I feel like, what did I have on…chinos? I think, were they chocolate? They were chocolate colored khakis.

Yeah, it was cool. And then the chunky Vans, the ’90s sort of Vans, silver, you’ll see them on the show all the time with a silver stripe on them. So you did help me out. I did not know what I was doing, and you were my most fashionable friend, so I needed support in that area.

Absolutely do not put the flamingo shirt on me. That is a hundred percent you, and I will not be accepting that.

Jon Wilde said, "That flamingo shirt belongs everywhere."

So that was another question I was going to ask, which is: Do you dress yourself for the show? Did you have to just bring three suitcases of clothes with you, or do they help dial in the Joe Vanella aesthetic?

So mainly we provide our own stuff. There’s no makeup people. There’s nothing like that. We dress ourselves. We get a little guidance because in the past there’s Housewives and they got Dolce Gabbana, they’ve got Chanel—and then I roll up and I got a bunch of Hanes Beefy-Ts and American Eagle jeans. It’s a very big switch. But yeah, that stuff, that’s mine. I love Hawaiian shirts, so it worked out well for me.

I am. Nothing says Hawaiian shirt climate like the mountains of the Scottish Highlands, right?

The most tropical place you can think of.

Absolutely. You’ve had some amazing moments. I would say you have been by far the most memed-slash-memeable contestant on this season of the Traitors. You kicked that off with a wink directly at the camera in episode one, and from then on, you’ve really manufactured a few wonderful ones. We’ll get to the apple in a moment, but what I wanted to talk about really briefly was the moment with Michael, who’s no longer on the show. You guys had a really lovely, beautiful moment where you were at the round table at the end of the day. You gave him some support in saying you did not think he was a Traitor. And then there’s this really beautiful moment afterwards where he—and I’m paraphrasing here—but as a gay man, he says he grew up with a bunch of guys who looked and sounded like you—a.k.a., an extremely Italian dude from the deepest parts of Long Island. And he says he did not get a lot of respect, and did not feel very supported by those people as a gay kid. And he told you how much he appreciated that you stepped out and offered him support. I’m interested in what that moment was like for you: if you expected that, if you two had built something up until then? And also, how much weight you feel representing Long Island, which does come with some comical, but not always so comical, stereotypes.

The Michael thing, when he came up to me in the Armory, I didn’t expect it at all. I defended Michael because I got to know Michael. Michael was my day-one. We were in the Land Rover together going into the castle. I knew him from the very beginning. And he dropped that on me. I didn’t think that I was doing anything except defending a friend at that point. It had nothing to do with gameplay. It’s just somebody I care about who I saw was kind of getting railroaded, and I wanted to step in and stick up for him. But when he came up to me and he hit me with that, I was so honored. It’s not anything that I ever expected, and it hit me in that moment. I’m like, man, I didn’t want him to think it was gameplay.

That was the most important thing. I didn’t want to come off as not genuine. I didn’t want him to get out of the game and be like, "Oh, this guy lied to me. What an asshole." So to have him feel that comfortable with me, to come up and share that moment with me, it just meant the world. And Michael and I are still such great friends. He’s truly one of my best friends to come out of that castle. I talk to him every day. He’s funny as hell. He’s a great human being, and it feels so awful to hear that he had such a tough go in his childhood, especially being a father myself. I don’t want any of my kids to feel that way. They’re free to love whatever way they want to love, and everybody should feel that way. And to hear that he had a negative time growing up, it hit me right in my gut.

Yeah, it was a really beautiful moment. You’ve mentioned maybe once or twice or 13 times that you’re from Long Island.

Yeah. Why won’t you let me be proud of where I’m from?

I want you to be proud. You’re clearly proud. I love that about you. You’ve always been proud to be from Long Island. You love the Jets and the Islanders. And so in that way, I’m like, this is not a thing people choose. This is a thing they’re obviously born into. But have you felt the need to represent Long Island in a better light? Is that fair to say? In a better-than-its-stereotype light?

Long Island gets a bad rap. Long Islanders get a bad rap. I think, what was it? What was the show with the Seavers? Was that Family Ties? Michael J. Fox was on it? They lived on the North Shore of Long Island. They represented great. And sometime between Family Ties and now, Long Islanders get this rap like we’re all loud oafs.

[Laughing] When I think of loud oafs, Joe Vanella is at the very bottom. But I came into the game and the most important thing, I wanted to show myself as somebody from Long Island who’s representing in a positive light. And people from Long Island have been so great and warm about backing me. My DMs are constantly filled with people saying, thank you for representing Long Island this way. And it warms my heart, because I love where I come from. I’m so proud. I think this is one of the greatest places to live. I think it’s one of the greatest places to raise kids. Everything that you want is here. It’s incredible. The people are awesome. Yes, they’re loud. Yes, they’re opinionated, but that doesn’t make them bad. It just makes them sure of who they are. And I think that’s a typical Long Islander.

And for what it’s worth, my dad is a Yankees, Giants, and Rangers fan, and I went against all his fandom to try and stick it to him, and it backfired totally against me.

Yeah, that was brutal. That was a horrible choice on your part. You, by trade, are a funeral director. You’ve now achieved a fascinating level of public fame. Are people-

You’re re-’Gramming people who are going as you for Halloween and you’ve not been canceled. That’s a pretty positive version of fame in 2026. It’s not easy to thread that needle these days. Have you-

People going as me as a Halloween costume is one of the craziest things that’s ever happened. It’s insane.

Have people recognized you while you were…funerarily directing? Has that happened yet?

Yes. In a couple of the funeral homes, I have been stopped and they’re like, "Hey, do you ever get that you look like... Are you Joe from the Traitors?" And I’m like, "Yeah." And they’ve stopped me for pictures. I hate to say it’s a fun thing because they’re in this time of awful grief and then they’re like, "Oh, they’re the loud guy from Traitors. Let’s grab a pic before we get into the limo." So it’s sort of providing them with a story and some humor before they head off to the funeral. So I’m glad to bring that to them in those situations.

What’s it like walking around and having people know you? I mean, a month and a half ago, nobody save the most blessed among us knew Joe Vanella. And now you can walk around and people are like, "Oh wow, it’s the Joe Vanella."

The first time it happened, I was in Penn Station and I was Googling how to get to wherever I was going, and this girl came up to me and she’s like, "Are you going to be on The Traitors?” I guess the cast was just released. And I’m like, "Yeah." And then she’s like, "Oh, can we take a picture with you?" And I’m like, "For what?" And then they said, "Well, you’re on The Traitors." And it took a minute. I’m like, "Oh, people actually want my picture." It’s completely, completely bonkers. I had one person come up to me and they’re like, "I’m so nervous." I’m like, "Why? Who cares? It’s me. What am I? Just take my picture. You’re fine. We can hang out." I was trick-or-treating with my kids, and I knocked on somebody’s house, and the guy came to the door and he’s like, "I was just watching you on the TV." And he called to his husband, and his husband came out and they’re like, "You’re literally on my TV right now.”

It’s crazy. It’s something I can’t wrap my head around because, like you said, six weeks ago, nobody really knew who I was. And now all of a sudden it’s like, "Hey, can I get your picture?” all the time. And it’s so cool, because I’ve always been a picture taker when I’ve seen anybody out who I recognize. I famously bothered Gina Gershon one night at a bar in, I think it was the Lower East Side, and she was an absolute sweetheart. But now people are doing that to me, I want to make sure that they walk away with a good opinion of me. And that’s what I’m trying to do. I’m trying to show them I am who I am on the show, even outside.

You want to pay it forward from Gina Gershon, as you rightly should. How does Meg, your wife, feel about this? She didn’t get a choice in this matter.

Well, listen, this whole thing without her never would’ve happened. I’m the luckiest guy. Today’s actually my anniversary.

Thank you. Thank you. I’m the luckiest guy in the world to have her because if she said no, if I couldn’t go to Scotland, I would’ve never had this opportunity. And she stepped up so big, took care of the kids, took care of everything that had to be at home, didn’t even hesitate. She goes, "If you get the chance, I want you to go." So she’s handling this well. Again, this is her favorite show too. Her biggest thing, when I came home from Scotland, she said she didn’t want to know anything. She didn’t know if I was a traitor. She loves the show so much that she wanted to be surprised all way around.

Was she surprised that you’re such a good liar? Is she feeling good about that? It turns out you’re a pretty solid liar. People believe that you’re a good guy when you’re out here murdering them night after night.

No, I’m done. I’m cooked as far as that goes. The facade is down. She knows when I’m lying at this point. She doesn’t trust me and she’s right not to. I mean, you see what I’m doing every week. I wouldn’t trust me either.

It turns out you’re spectacularly good at lying and you’ve let the whole world know about it. It seems like maybe misplaying your hand, but it’s working out for you. Earlier, we briefly touched on your athletic ability, your prowess. It’s not been great. Certainly the show spent a few moments within the scope of the challenges showing you splayed out, just really sucking air. And I wondered how that felt, seeing yourself laid out on the ground just like a fish on a pier.

So if you watch that scene... Now, first of all, we’re not even going to get into the fact that as time’s expiring, I flew through the air like a Michael Jordan poster from 1993, dunking the bag of money into the barrel. I should be a poster in children’s bedrooms at this point, just gracefully flying. But at that particular moment, I was lying on the ground and I remember looking up at the sky, and if you watch it, at first I’m distressed, but then I’m kind of smiling. As I’m collecting myself to continue to live, I looked up at the sky like, "How the hell did I get here?" It was such a great experience, and I was just in it at that moment, and realizing the gravity of everything, as exhausted as I was. And yeah, my cardio, not great, not great. I got a five-year-old, a four-year-old, and a two-year-old. I don’t have time to go to the gym. My cardio is chasing them around the house. So at that particular moment, sweating next to a barrel in the Highlands of Scotland, I’m just like, man. It all hit me at once, and I’m just having the time of my life.

I feel like we’ve got to really quickly talk about the apple. Obviously, the other big, big meme, and why people are dressing like you: As a traitor, you had to murder someone by throwing fruit to them. Hard episode to watch, because I was like, "Wow, only Victor’s catching onto this?” The edit made it seem really obvious what you were up to. And what came out of that, across several episodes, besides what Victor termed “Fruitgate”, was you having to say the word “roughage” a lot as defense for why you were suddenly so obsessed with having an apple. But have you been eating more apples and roughage? Did that change your own approach to roughage and apples?

Jon, I never want to see another apple in my life.

I went to a wedding yesterday, somebody tossed an apple at me. It’s like an everyday occurrence now. But what I want to point out is how important the social aspect of gameplay is there, because what was going on with Victor at that particular moment…Victor and I have very different styles. Victor’s very analytical. He’s good at what he does in that way. I’m very social. I’d pick up gummy bears and throw them at Mark. Mark would catch them in his mouth. I’d pick up beef jerky, which is constant. I was tossing something to somebody all the time. So now-

You treat everybody like they’re a Labrador retriever?

Exactly. Listen, I’m telling you, Mark would win best in show if he ever tried in Madison Square Garden. But everybody’s coming down on Morgan. They’re like, "Morgan, you don’t remember catching an apple?" Well, one, my social game I feel was strong enough that nobody’s antenna was up on me at that point—except for Victor, because Victor and I had beefed, going back to the Michael thing, going back before that. And Morgan knows me as somebody who’s playful, knows me as somebody who throws things around the castle, so she probably didn’t think anything of it. Joe’s just goofing off. That’s what I was doing.

What was the original question? I definitely talked too much.

Mostly just, are you eating apples and roughage?

Yeah, I’m trying to. My daughter has been shaming me. She’s like, "Dad, you need to eat more fruits and vegetables," even though she doesn’t eat any fruits and vegetables herself. So I have been trying to eat more. I’ve found a particular type of apple that I love. I think it’s called Snapdragon or something like that, and it’s very spicy. There’s an apple orchard or an apple place out in Syosset over here that I go to and I get them, and they’re fantastic. So I have been eating more apples.

If nothing else, that’s a win. What do you-

Do you know how much haggis binds you up? The normal American hasn’t had haggis. I ate about three tons of haggis when I was in Scotland. It’s like cement, but it tastes great. People want to rag on haggis. I know in Armageddon, one of the greatest movies of all time, there’s a haggis joke in it. You do need apples to move that stuff around in your stomach, otherwise you’re going to have a real hard time.

Got it. So it really was the haggis we’re looking at as the problem. Were they serving haggis in the castle?

Yeah. It’s Scotland, baby. You get haggis all the time.

Were you the only person eating haggis? It’s not a thing most people coming from the U.S. are into.

A lot of people were shying away. But you know what? They’re just not adventurous.

I know we’ve got to wrap up in a minute, but I do have to ask you: we go back a ways, known you more than 20 years. Part of that has been we’ve had-

Did I drive you into Brooklyn when you moved there the first time? I feel like I did.

We listened to Wu-Tang clan and I moved you into Brooklyn.

How else could we do it? So, most of the time we have spent as friends, we’ve also been in a fantasy baseball league, of which you’ve been commissioner. We’ve had our differences in terms of your commissioning style. But as I think you remember, I won the championship this year.

That’s right. Anyways, thank you for the interview. It’s been a pleasure.

Because I was in Alan’s castle for a period of time during this season. We’re going to leave that out.

I’m sorry you lost this season. It’s been a pleasure speaking to you. I’ll see you, I don’t know…I’ll see you on my TV, I guess.

#6673. Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

Chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a new personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

#6672. Ariana Grande and Ricky Alvarez’s Full Relationship Timeline

Nearly a decade after ending their relationship, Ariana Grande and Ricky Alvarez are back in the public eye.

The former couple recently sparked reconciliation rumors after they were spotted spending time together in Texas and Florida during Grande’s Eternal Sunshine Tour. Grande also made multiple changes to the Ricky lyric in “Thank U, Next,” prompting fans to wonder whether the pair had rekindled their romance.

On July 14, People confirmed that they were back on—but taking things slowly. “Ariana has always considered Ricky a friend,” a source told People. “She’s not held ill will against him [since their split]. Ricky is dependable, trustworthy and very supportive. Ariana feels she can be herself around Ricky.”

Grande and Alvarez first met when he joined her as a backup dancer on her 2015 Honeymoon Tour. They dated for about a year before separating in 2016, but have maintained a friendly relationship ever since.

Below, a full timeline of everything we know about Ariana Grande and Ricky Alvarez’s relationship.

Grande and Alvarez met while he worked as a backup dancer on her Honeymoon Tour. They began dating that year.

Grande briefly spoke about their relationship in a Billboard cover story.

“We’re happy,” she said. “I’m a very happy girl. I have a healthy life right now, and I think that’s all anyone cares to know. The end.”

The story also included comments from Grande’s friend Victoria Monét, who shared that “Moonlight” was inspired by the beginning of Grande and Alvarez’s relationship.

“That’s what Ricky called her one night,” Monét said. “I think it was after their first kiss. He waited to kiss her for a long time, and she was really impressed. He’s such a gentleman, and the song is a great little bookmark of the start of their relationship.”

Multiple outlets reported that Grande and Alvarez had ended their relationship after about a year together.

Grande referenced Alvarez in her hit single “Thank U, Next,” singing, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / Now I listen and laugh.”

After the song’s release, Alvarez shared videos of himself reacting to the lyric on Instagram Stories.

“Nothing but gratitude,” he wrote. “Thank you, next… (those songs are fire tho… you’re welcome).”

Grande reposted his Stories and joked about the lyric herself.

“HAHAHAHAHHAHAHAH IM SORRY U GOT THE WORST LINE. It was meant v lovingly.”

When fans later speculated that the pair had reunited after they interacted on Instagram, Grande shut down the rumors herself in the comments of one of Alvarez’s posts.

“We’re friends, everyone take a big ol breather,” she wrote.

Years later, Grande and Alvarez were photographed together in Austin, Texas, ahead of one of her Eternal Sunshine Tour stops. Photos circulating online showed them dining with a group while Grande celebrated her birthday in the city.

According to TMZ, sources familiar with the situation said Alvarez was one of several friends spending time with Grande and that the outing was purely platonic. People also reported that the pair had “been hanging out recently.”

During her Austin concerts, Grande also made noticeable changes to the Ricky lyric in “Thank U, Next.”

Earlier in the week, she sang, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / And they still kinda slap.” At another performance, she changed the line again, singing, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / I know he’s still got my back.”

Over Fourth of July weekend, Grande and Alvarez were photographed shopping together at a Whole Foods in Boca Raton, Florida, before heading to celebrate the holiday with Grande’s family, according to TMZ.

The outing came after Grande wrapped three sold-out Eternal Sunshine Tour shows in nearby Sunrise.

The following day, People published additional details about their friendship, citing a source who said Alvarez has been joining Grande for portions of her tour.

“She’s having a great time on tour. She loves having close friends join her for parts of the tour,” the source said. “Ricky has always been a friend and confidant. She really trusts him. He has such great, positive energy, makes her laugh, and she enjoys spending time with him.”

The source also addressed Grande’s life following her breakup from Ethan Slater.

“Her relationship with Ethan is 100 percent over. She’s focused on her tour and spending time with the people who have always been there for her,” the source said. “Ariana is having the best time reconnecting with fans and loves being onstage.”

Grande fueled reconciliation rumors herself a week later on July 13. She changed the Ricky lyric of “Thank U, Next” again during her Brooklyn show, singing, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / We always find our way back.”

Hours later on July 14, sources confirmed to People and TMZ that they were officially dating again. The insiders told both outlets that they were taking things very slowly.

“They’re not jumping into anything serious right away, but Ari is happy to have him back in her life,” a source told People. The insider added that they “have a similar, smart, dry sense of humor.”

On July 16, Grande and Alvarez were photographed walking in Central Park with their arms wrapped around each other. It marked their first public sighting since news of their reconciliation broke.

On July 17, TMZ shared more pictures of the couple enjoying some PDA from the same day. In the images, Alvarez is embracing Grande as she leans toward him on the street.

Alvarez went out and supported Grande while she performed in Brooklyn. The dancer was spotted at her July 18 and 19 Eternal Sunshine Tour shows. On the second night, he and Grande’s brother, Frankie Grande, had a sweet moment.

On July 27, Grande soft-launched her relationship with Alvarez on Instagram. The singer tagged him in a Polaroid of herself, seemingly giving him credit for taking it.

On August 12, Grande went Instagram official with Alvarez, sharing two photos of them together in a carousel post. “🌱 ！ ♡,” she captioned it.

Days after Grande made her relationship with Alvarez Instagram official, fans noticed that the couple appears to share a meaningful tattoo. During the London stop of her Eternal Sunshine Tour, Grande displayed a new piece across her upper chest reading, “I do love you.” Alvarez has the same phrase tattooed near his collarbone, though his version appears in a different typeface.

A few days later, they were seen in London, where Grande was set to start her 10-day residency. The couple was wearing two cozy layered looks in the cooler U.K. temperatures, with Grande wearing an oversize white cardigan and Alvarez in a jean jacket. They walked arm-in-arm down the street, immersed in conversation.

Grande and Alvarez were also photographed out in London with Grande’s mom, Joan, on August 27. In the photos, Grande and Alvarez walked hand-in-hand as they made their way through the city.

Grande wore a fitted white graphic T-shirt with dark-wash jeans, oversize sunglasses, and a white headband, while Alvarez kept things casual in a white T-shirt, jeans, and a baseball cap. Joan joined them in an all-black look with pink earrings.

During the final show of her Eternal Sunshine Tour at London’s O2 Arena, Grande gave Alvarez another shout-out while performing “Thank U, Next.”

When she reached the lyric about her boyfriend, she changed the original line to, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / I’m tryna make him my last.”

That same week, Alvarez shared his photos from Grande’s tour, including one of her kissing his hand in what appears to be a dressing room. He otherwise captured her in motion, performing onstage.

“It’s the best thing to do,” he wrote in the caption.

The post comes shortly after Grande shared a snippet of them kissing at her rehearsals in London. The intimate moment was part of a video montage she shared at the end of her Eternal Sunshine Tour to thank everyone for what she calls “one of the most beautiful, extraordinary experiences” of her life.

On November 7, Grande shared an Instagram Reel with Alvarez as the couple played a kissing challenge game for her makeup brand, R.E.M. Beauty.

In the video, Grande sat on Alvarez’s lap while he wore a beanie over his eyes and attempted to guess what lip product she was wearing when she kissed him.

“This is a challenge called ‘What’s on my lips?’” Grande explained.

“Or what’s on my girlfriend’s lips, really,” Alvarez quipped.

The dancer correctly identified several products, including an unreleased shade called Holiday Mélange.

A few days later, on November 11, Alvarez and Grande made their red carpet debut at the New York City premiere of Focker-In-Law.

Grande chose a vintage Badgley Mischka gown with a fitted bodice and full plaid skirt, while Alvarez wore a black blazer over a white shirt with dark jeans.

#6671. Sneak Inside GQ’s Breakouts House Party Deep in the Hollywood Hills

GQ’s Breakouts have officially broken containment. Last night, high up in the Hollywood hills, at one of LA’s most famous spots—the glass-and-concrete modernist sculpture known as the Sheats-Goldstein residence—GQ toasted to a new class of stars who spent 2026 commanding our attention.

First, they had to get in—down the palm-lined path, past the apple-red twin-engined car brought by presenting sponsor Hot Wheels, across the mildly perilous path over a koi pond—to a tucked-away den where GQ Editor-in-chief Adam Baidawi quickly toasted the 13 Breakouts of 2026. “The double edged sword of success is that sometimes you’re so out-of-your mind busy and stressed and locked in, that you forget to enjoy it,” he told the room. “I hope you find a moment to enjoy it tonight.” And then he laid out the evening’s goals: have a hell of a house party. Everyone obliged.

GQ Breakouts Stavros Halkias and Pablo Torre huddled with Hasan Piker, who later chatted with Jake Shane, creating a powerful personality vortex. Amelia Dimoldenberg sipped an espresso martini at the bar in the house’s club. Breakout Belmont Cameli hung out poolside on the terrace, soaking up cinematic views of a glittering LA, while DJ Alice Longyu Gao played classic bangers like Drake and Future’s “Diamonds Dancing” filled the air. Later, towards the end of the night, two guests went rogue and got themselves escorted out for diving into the pool in their underwear. (In a shocking twist, it was not Stav, who had shouted “Cannonball!” earlier, by the house’s other pool.) Houseparty’s gonna houseparty.

When I found GQ Breakout Pablo Torre outside, he was showing off the incredible business card that house owner Jimmy Goldstein had given him just moments before. It was huge, about the size of an index card you used to study for algebra tests. Rare memorabilia.

Torre—who made the NBA’s life difficult with reporting that blew open the Kawhi Leonard scandal—joked to me that Clippers fandom is so tepid in LA that he hardly felt like he had to watch his back while in town from New York. (The biggest concern for his visit: a rainy forecast for the weekend.)

As Breakout AZ Chike told GQ for his portfolio interview, people “crossed worlds that hadn’t been crossed before.” Chike parlayed fellow Breakout Cameli early in the night before taking the stage a few hours later to run through heaters like “Packed Up” and “Look Like My Mama”—the same tracks that earned him GQ Breakout status. He told me he’s enjoying being back home in LA after touring his new album across the country, playing in new-for-him cities. Turns out DC showed an unexpected amount of love to a West Coast kid.

GQ Breakout Owen Thiele celebrated the season 3 renewal of Adults—announced earlier in the day—by zipping around the party armed with a disposable film camera. Watching him connect with True Whitaker of I Love LA felt like witnessing the cinematic crossover that we lowkey need to see play out on-screen.

Mavi, the North Carolina rapper who popped up in GQ’s September best new music portfolio, told me he’s finishing the project that he teased back then. He says he has so many songs in the tuck that he might thank his fans by dropping more than we’d expect.

Speaking of fresh music from new talents, Leon Thomas said he isn’t tripping expectations for his follow-up to the critically acclaimed, Grammy-winning “Mutt,” and previewed a project that’ll source inspiration from “p-funk, soul, and hip-hop.” Thomas was in the midst of rehearsing for an appearance at Tyler, The Creator’s Flog Gnaw festival this weekend, and joked that he got so sweaty during practice that we can expect him to tear it down on Saturday.

For the moment though, the weather was perfect, the music was hitting, the vibes were strong, and there was a lot more night left for partying. See how it all went down below. ✦

#6669. Ariana Grande Brings Her Two Great Loves—Ricky Álvarez and Rare Vintage—to the Red Carpet

Ariana Grande brought two of her greatest loves to the red carpet last night: boyfriend Ricky Álvarez and a very, very good piece of vintage.

At the New York premiere of Focker-in-Law, the singer and actor made her first red carpet appearance with Álvarez since rekindling their romance earlier this year. And if their constant embraces, adoring glances, and kisses were anything to go by, the pair are very much still in the honeymoon phase.

Stylist Law Roach selected a vintage 1990s Badgley Mischka gown for the occasion. The delicate, spaghetti-strapped design featured a pale silver-gray windowpane check, a fitted bodice scattered with tiny beaded flowers, and a voluminous floor-skimming skirt. She accessorized with Swarovski Matrix hoop earrings—a recent favorite—and traded the flipped bob she’s been sporting of late for a sleek micro ponytail, tied with a little ivory ribbon. Makeup was also her go-to style of glowy and highlight-dominant.

Roach is on a particularly impressive archival streak of late. He’s been mining the fashion vaults for Kim Kardashian’s All's Fair press tour, pulling everything from 1990s Dolce & Gabbana to Paco Rabanne couture. Just last weekend, he dressed Anya Taylor-Joy in a spectacularly ruffled spring 1997 Pierre Cardin ensemble for the LACMA Art+Film Gala.

Grande has long been a devotee of fashion’s more whimsical, romantic history. Her love of vintage reached particularly fanciful heights during the Wicked press tours, but the singer has since held firmly to her soft, ultra-feminine aesthetic with 1950s silhouettes and diaphanous fabrics. At one point, her dedication to the look was so pronounced that some wondered whether she was quietly auditioning for a rumored Audrey Hepburn biopic. Roach revealed that he’d bought the Badgley Mischka gown months earlier, drawn to its connection with the era of the original Meet the Parents film.

Álvarez, for his part, kept things considerably more low-key. The dancer and photographer wore a relaxed black blazer over an open-neck white shirt, tucked into dark indigo jeans with rolled cuffs, a leather belt, and brown shoes. Some classic easy-going boyfriend dressing. He spent much of the evening with an arm around Grande’s waist, while she leaned into him, held his hands, and beamed up at him for the cameras.

Of course, the couple’s love story has its own history. Grande and Álvarez first met when he worked as a backup dancer on her Honeymoon Tour in 2015. They dated for around a year before splitting in 2016, and he later received a memorable name-check in her 2018 breakup anthem, “thank u, next.” Almost a decade later, however, things have come full circle. Rumors of a reunion began circulating this summer when the pair were spotted together in Austin, Texas, during Grande’s Eternal Sunshine tour, before more sightings followed in Florida and New York. By August, they were Instagram official, and Grande had debuted a new tattoo reading “I do love you”, seemingly matching a similar inscription on Álvarez’s collarbone. The two were also spotted arm-in-arm around London, where Grande completed her 10-night residency at the O2. She even began rewriting the Ricky lyrics in “thank u, next” onstage. At one Brooklyn show, she sang, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / We always find our way back.” By the tour’s September finale in London, the sentiment had become considerably more definitive: “I’m tryna make him my last.”

More recently, they’ve been enjoying some more ordinary couple activities, including cheering on runners at the New York City Marathon earlier this month. Grande has also enlisted Álvarez for a particularly kiss-heavy R.E.M. Beauty lip-product guessing game on Instagram. The adoration and affection is showing no signs of slowing down.

Between a decade-old romance finding new life and a beautiful dress pulled from the archives, Ariana Grande is making a persuasive case for revisiting the past.

#6668. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

Netflix’s deadly, dark, and irreverently funny spy thriller follows a covert intelligence organization as it uncovers and sells secrets among the rich and powerful. Season 1 brought us Keira Knightley as the fearless agent Helen; Sarah Lancashire as her icy spymaster, Reed; and Ben Whishaw as an assassin and Helen’s longtime friend.

That first season closed with many loose ends, so it wasn’t a huge surprise when it was announced that we’d be seeing Helen and Sam in action again. Now, season 2 has brought the pair back to our screens, with a handful of fresh faces to add to the drama. This time around, Sam appears as a washed-up hit man taking low-paid jobs, while Helen is still working for the Black Doves—something that proves to be complicated given her husband, Wallace (played by Andrew Buchan), is now prime minister.

All episodes of the new season dropped on Netflix on November 5. If you’re eager to get to know the cast and characters more closely—and are wondering where you might have seen those new faces before—then read on.

As an agent of the Black Doves, Helen Webb is tasked with gathering highly sensitive information obtained via her politician husband, Wallace. But keeping up the image of a good spouse, mother, and spy all at once becomes increasingly difficult to maintain, and Helen grows conflicted about her life of betrayal. You’ll know Keira Knightley, of course, from her career of starry roles in everything from Disney’s Pirates of the Caribbean to Pride & Prejudice, Bend It Like Beckham, and Love Actually.

Helen’s close friend, a previously high-flying hit man, an ex-employee of the Black Doves, Sam Young attempted to leave behind his former life—but that was easier said than done. Now he’s taking low-paid jobs and drinking alone in bars, before he finds himself roped into business with Helen once again. You’ll know Whishaw from his role in Daniel Craig’s James Bond films—Skyfall, Spectre, and No Time to Die—as well as A Very English Scandal and The Hour.

Relentless and cold, the spymaster Reed is Helen’s handler at the Black Doves and does not mess around. In season 2, we see new, more vulnerable sides of her character unfold via glimpses of her younger self and flashes to the past events that came to define her. You’ll recognize Lancashire from her role in Happy Valley.

Wallace Webb is Helen’s husband and the father of her two children, and he’s completely unaware of her career as a Black Dove. In season 2, his own career has taken off and he becomes the U.K.’s prime minister—a move that comes with highly strict security measures in the backdrop of rising tensions in his marriage. Buchan has also starred in Industry, The Crown, and Carnival Row.

Another assassin, Williams, worked for the crime leader Lenny in the first season of Black Doves.
