Hyland has starred in Towards Zero, A Thousand Blows, and Tall Tales and Murder.

As Williams’s partner, Eleanor is another fast-footed assassin with a refreshing sense of humor. Creevy has also starred in Amadeus, The Guest, and Operation Mincemeat.

Laila is an assassin with a fun, nonchalant, and lighthearted personality—a contrast to Helen, whom she clashes with at the start of season 2. You’ll know Ambika Mod for her roles in This Is Going to Hurt and as the co-lead of Netflix’s One Day adaptation.

Mr. Conteh is a senior at Black Doves and is hungry for power. As the fabric of the institution is put under pressure and he is sent to investigate Reed, Conteh becomes increasingly prominent for Helen and her associates. Ceesay has also starred in Alien: Earth.

Cruelly minded and understated in tone, Patrick works for a rival organization to Black Doves, the same group that presents an appealing get-out for Sam when he needs it the most. Riley also starred in the comedy-horror Pride and Prejudice and Zombies as well as Firebrand.

Hard-headed with tunnel vision, Cecile Mason is a U.S. defense envoy, arriving at 10 Downing Street to work on relations between the president and the prime minister ahead of a major peace summit. Campbell was a star of the Scream movies, as well as Party of Five and Wild Things.

Glamorous and sharp-minded, Katia Chernov is the wife of Russian oligarch Alexi Chernov and becomes swept up in the mysteries in the new series. She’s played by Sylvia Hoeks, who has also starred in Blade Runner 2049 and The Girl in the Spider’s Web.

A well-connected Russian oligarch with immeasurable influence and power, Alexi Chernov is a force to be reckoned with in season 2, with fingers in some of the most fragile cases. He’s played by Goran Kostić, whom you may recognize from Ant-Man and the Wasp or Canary Black.

#6664. Kim Kardashian Plays Nurse in One of Louis Vuitton’s Rarest Runway Looks

Kim Kardashian has been raiding the fashion archives with extraordinary enthusiasm of late, but her latest vintage pull comes with a health warning. Enter: a very rare, almost 20-year-old Louis Vuitton nurse uniform, complete with a monogrammed lace face mask, personalized cap, and coordinating accessories. The look, from Marc Jacobs’s spring 2008 collection for the house, is a heart-palpitating piece of runway history.

The ensemble was sourced by stylist Law Roach from the personal archive of Lauren Pyes, a Boston-based Harvard University employee and avid collector of Jacobs-era Louis Vuitton, whose extraordinary collection Vogue first explored last year. Pyes has spent years scouring resale platforms, boutiques, and obscure corners of the internet for some of the designer’s most coveted creations, amassing what she affectionately calls the “Marchive.”

“Law reached out to me a few months ago and was interested in pieces of the Marchive," Pyes tells Vogue. “Suffice to say, I was thrilled to loan them to him.” When Roach first contacted her, she could scarcely believe it was him. “I kept toggling back and forth to make sure it wasn’t a spam account!” she recalls. “Although he has a larger-than-life public persona, Law is deeply kind and gracious in addition to being the visionary he is rightly lauded as. I have so much respect for his dedication to telling stories through fashion and his commitment to finding the pieces that do exactly that.”

And few collections have quite as much storytelling potential as Louis Vuitton’s spring 2008 offering. Presented in Paris in October 2007, the show opened with a procession of supermodels—including Naomi Campbell, Stephanie Seymour, Eva Herzigova, and Nadja Auermann—dressed as nurses in sheer, pastel-colored uniforms, black lace masks, and white caps. The inspiration was the American artist Richard Prince, whose provocative Nurse Paintings informed the collection and accompanying collaboration with the house. Reviewing the collection at the time, Vogue’s Sarah Mower described it as a “typical Jacobs coup of multidimensional, referential, and self-referential significance,” and a “hilariously kinky parade” that “reflected Jacobs’s way of walking the line between creative freedom and commercial innovation.” It was one of Jacobs’s most deviant, deliciously strange runway spectacles.

The shoes from Louis Vuitton spring 2028.

The full look, as sourced by Lauren Pyes.

Kim Kardashian’s interpretation was remarkably faithful to the original. She wore the sheer, short-sleeved white nurse’s coat cinched at the waist over a delicate, peach-colored silk dress, with white stockings and peep-toe heels. A black lace Louis Vuitton face mask covered her mouth, while a white nurse’s cap (commissioned by Roach and reimagined by legendary milliner Stephen Jones) bearing a red “K” sat atop her sleek dark hair. In her arms was another treasure from the collection: an Aquarelle Papillon bag. The shoes also hailed from spring 2008.

Bringing together such a complete ensemble was no small undertaking. “I sourced these pieces from all over—including platforms like Poshmark and Vestiaire Collective—for over a year,” Pyes explains. The dresses have become a particular obsession: she has owned four, including a pink silk satin version that remains in her permanent collection. Vogue actually purchased another of the orange dresses—the same color Kardashian wore—from Pyes a little over a year ago. But the real rarity is the mask and overcoat, which Pyes considers among her most treasured finds. Earlier this year, the ensemble was exhibited at the Savannah College of Art and Design (SCAD), where it even caught the attention of one of its original creators.

“I had it exhibited at SCAD back in April, and Stephen Jones—who made it in collaboration with Louis Vuitton—was apparently surprised that it even existed!” Pyes says of the mask. “If the person who made it was in disbelief by seeing it, I guess that means it is pretty rare!”

Kardashian and Roach have been on a formidable archival streak throughout the All’s Fair press tour, resurrecting everything from ’90s Paco Rabanne couture to vintage Dolce & Gabbana and Jean Paul Gaultier-era Hermès. The Louis Vuitton nurse look is their most playful fashion deep dive yet.

And for Pyes, it’s precisely that irreverence that makes the Jacobs years so compelling. She points to the extraordinary creative team behind the collection, including Peter Copping, then head of womenswear and now creative director of Lanvin, and Camille Miceli, currently at the helm of Pucci. “This collection and these pieces are so special because they highlight what Marc and his team did so well—seamlessly integrating fashion and art into a cohesive and powerful narrative,” she says. She remembers the supermodel casting, the nurse uniforms, and even Jacobs taking his final bow beside a custom Vuitton trunk playing an episode of SpongeBob SquarePants. “There are so many elements that were unexpected and genuine in a pre-social media age.”

Pyes, of course, has continued to do some killer sourcing. She’s recently completed a “trifecta of accessories” from the Louis Vuitton fall 2011 collection, better known as the “Fetish Collection.” This includes a shearling porter hat, mask hair accessory, and a patent leather bib. On the non-vintage side of things? “I am champing at the bit to receive the custom order I put in from Marc’s Spring 2027 collection,” she shares. “After more than 40 years, he continues to create incredible fashion and I feel fortunate to be adding this ensemble to the Marchive!”

Whether Kim’s look was a Halloween latergram, another cheeky press tour outing, or just a moment of play inside an impressive archive, for now, is anyone’s guess. Whatever the occasion, Pyes is delighted to see the collection enjoying a new life in the public imagination. Nearly two decades after its debut, Jacobs’s peculiar, provocative vision remains as potent as ever. “These clothes are not just beautiful and special,” she says, “but also consequential. This collection walked almost 20 years ago and yet continues to figure so largely in pop culture and the imagination of fashion lovers.” Nurse Kardashia, the defibrillator please!

#6663. Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

#6662. Best Men’s Winter Parkas 2026: 17 Heavy-Duty Snow-Busting Coats

The best men's parka is a lot like an upright sleeping bag, except it doesn't simply keep you insulated. It also protects your frostbite-prone fits from Mother Nature’s icy clutches, and keeps you looking sharp in the process. Don't believe us? Just ask the parka's most loyal servant: Oasis frontman Liam Gallagher.

Before giving you our favourites, some quick history: Parkas originated in the Arctic, where the Inuit designed them to withstand bone-chilling temperatures. They then made their way to the US military with the introduction of the N-3B parka in the 1950s. Throughout its evolution, the parka's mission has remained unchanged: to keep not just your torso warm, but your thighs and rear end too. Seriously, you've already worn that waist-length puffer to death: Make like Justin Jefferson. Go long.

The North Face McMurdo down parka isn’t just another winter coat—it’s a cold-weather icon with Antarctic-level credibility. Named after McMurdo Station, the US research hub in Antarctica, this parka is designed to thrive in below-freezing temperatures while keeping you comfortable and protected. With 600-fill recycled down insulation and windproof, waterproof, and breathable DryVent technology, it’s eco-friendly armor for the tundra—or the Target parking lot. Made from recycled nylon and polyester, it’s part of The North Face’s recycled-repurpose collection, combining sustainability with serious performance.

Loaded with features like six exterior pockets, a removable faux-fur ruff, an adjustable hood, and a draft flap, this 3.5-pound powerhouse is your portable fortress of warmth. Stylish touches like the midnight petrol color elevate it above standard winter fare, while practical details make it indispensable for everything from scraping windshields to tackling arctic adventures. Whether you’re braving brutal weather or commuting in comfort, the McMurdo is built to last—complete with The North Face’s warranty to keep it in the game longer than your ever-disappearing gloves.

Mountain Hardwear has been a staple in the outdoor gear world long before its sold-out collaboration with Stüssy (though they’ve probably gained a few new fans in the process). Founded in 1993 in Richmond, California, the brand spun off from the well-known outdoor company Sierra Designs. A group of designers and engineers left Sierra Designs to create Mountain Hardwear, and 32 years later, it’s still famous for its technical outerwear, sleeping bags, and pioneering use of Gore-Tex.

This jacket is built for camping, featuring a durable ripstop shell and 650-fill down. With a fully adjustable insulated hood and a drawcord at the waist to trap in heat, it’s tough to top even before you encounter the two BYO-bevvy pockets—specially designed to carry your favorite beverages. Whether you're in your tent or Air Streamer, this jacket keeps you warm—and your drinks cold—so you can stay cozy and hydrated in style.

Woolrich: So good it doesn't need a logo patch. The American outdoor company was founded in 1830, and since then has become the destination for warmth-minded men who don't need anyone else to know they're walking around in the very best materials.

Which isn't to say this parka won't turn some heads. New for this season, it comes in seven colors, from a stunning light blue to nutty falcon brown, and also boasts some envy-inducing hand-warmer pockets, hidden rib-knit cuffs, and even a water-repellent finish. (A nice touch for a style that typically is more preoccupied with keeping out the cold than the wet.) One more thing: It's called the Cloud because it's incredibly light, even with a 90/10 duck down fill. A winter coat that wears like a summer-weight hoodie? Worth the investment.

This is the kind of Canada Goose jacket that reminds you why the brand is so much more than just a status symbol for finance guys. (Though I'm sure they don't mind being that too.) For one, it's done away with that ubiquitous blue and red logo, and replaced it with a more understated, tonal patch. But that's actually the only thing that's been stripped back here: Otherwise, this parka is packed full of features, from ribbed knit cuffs, to pockets everywhere you look, to a bevy of insulation considerations, from the 625 Fill Down interior all the way to the soft, lined chin guard—a nice touch.

Available this season in Black, Olive, and Desert Sand (above), it's backed by Canada Goose's lifetime guarantee. So, yes, you're spending a fortune. But the brand stands ready to make sure you'll never need to buy another parka again.

The Japanese label FrizmWORKS has reimagined a classic, ‘60s‐era expedition parka silhouette—quilted down, hard-wearing cotton-blend shell, boxy hooded cut—and, sixty years later, given it a whole new life. From the tonal matte finish to the utilitarian drawcord hem, this is a mountain‐camp relic reimagined for your 2025 commute. It’s rugged without resorting to SSX Tricky branding, and along with the requisite down filling also has two fun, unexpected and large pockets on the back. It also comes in a joyful orange color, if that black is a little too subtle for you.

I can't be the only one who was excited to see Reigning Champ get back into making real clothes. (Though, let’s be honest, the brand’s sweatsuits are still some of my favorites.) But this high-powered, goose-filled nylon parka? It's built for Canadian winters, which means it’ll easily thrive anywhere else, too. Technically, that means 700 fill power down, and a weather-repellent nylon shell to keep out wind and rain, as well as the colder temps. Its defining feature is its stealthy, all-black appearance, and Reigning Champ has leant hard into that vibe, with hidden interior pockets, concealed rib cuffs, and a shock cord hood that you can pull as tight as you like. Now you see me, now you don't.

The new kids on the parka block, Big Rock Candy Mountaineering, are bringing the fun back with their vibrant, winter parka colors. These extreme cold-weather parkas take inspiration from mid-century American outdoor brands. Can’t think of any off the top of your head? Skim through a book like this, and you’ll catch the vibe.

BRCM’s parkas are packed with cozy duck down and feature a 100% grosgrain shell. This ribbed texture, courtesy of its tight weave, makes the fabric tough as nails and resistant to wear and tear. The ginormous pockets? Perfect for stashing your winter accessories (or your snacks). And if the wind has you feeling like it’s got something to prove, just tighten up the drawstring waist, hood, and hem. One of the coolest features? The jacket’s silhouette. When cinched, you can clasp your bag around the waist—ideal for those who love a good backpacking adventure. Although BRCM is still a fresh face in the outerwear world, it already feels like an instant classic.

Getting your hands on one of the first-ever parkas is basically impossible—right up there with finding your keys when you’re already late. Enter The Real McCoy’s, which somehow pulls it off with museum-grade reproductions. Every detail is obsessively dialed, down to the DuPont-developed nylon shell that helped kick off the whole modern-materials era.

Today’s outdoor companies are still trying to capture Patagonia’s lightning-in-a-bottle formula from when the brand first burst onto the scene: Be nice to everyone, make products the right way, and design jackets built to last forever. Take its Glacier parka, for example: it’s weatherproof, cozy enough to double as a sleeping bag, and so comfortable you might consider skipping the tent altogether.

If you’re after a quieter, minimalist parka—and you’ve got the budget—the Therme Parka delivers. It’s hip-length, packed with goose down, and built with the brand’s more environmentally friendly GORE-TEX ePE fabric, meaning it’s primed to handle a lifetime of winters.

The Alpha Industries N-3B is the real-deal snorkel parka—because it is the real deal. Produced early in the company's history in the 1950s, the parka is still tough as nails and loaded with reinforced elbow patches, a full-length storm flap, and snug inset knit cuffs that keep wind firmly in its place.

Founded in 1960, Fjällräven are sort of Sweden's Patagonia. By which we mean they've always thought about three things: High-performance materials, a reasonable enough price point, and dressing it all up in some great primary colors.

Nanga is your favorite outerwear brand’s favorite outerwear brand. Its parka riffs on the US Air Force’s N-3B flight jacket, upgraded with AuroraTex—a high-performance fabric that keeps you dry no matter what. Add handwarmer pockets and a discreet cigar pouch, and you’ve got a parka that nails the perfect blend between utility and style.

Goldwin is so good, it literally owns the North Face in Japan. (Like, literally.) This handsome down parka is wind-blocking, body-warming, and equipped with a PERTEX Quantum ripstop lining (and shell) to prevent the tears and rips that lightweight fabrics can otherwise be prone to.

Berghaus' Meru jacket—which is long enough to qualify as a parka in our book—is packed with retro styling, from the color blocks to the cinchable waistband. 2L Gore-Tex means you could wear it up any peak, but its general aura means you could also wear it up on stage, hands behind your back, tambourine on your head.

Montbell's mastery of lightweight, easy-to-rock, nicely-priced outdoors gear has become its calling card, and it’s on full display here. This down parka is easy to incorporate into pretty much any wardrobe, and even has some nice-looking stitching (which, by the way, the heads call ‘baffling’).

What do you get when you cross a parka with a fireman jacket? A full-scale compliment magnet.

First and foremost: functionality. A great parka should incorporate more features than a midnight infomercial. In the outer shell, you’ll typically find materials like nylon or polyester, and sometimes more rugged options like Gore-Tex. But it's also worth peeking under the hood—literally. Parkas are usually filled with down (duck or goose feathers) or synthetic insulation like polyester. Down is warm and lightweight, but it’s the fair-weather friend of insulation—it falters when wet. Synthetic insulations, on the other hand, is the ride-or-die option, keeping you warm even when soggy.

Hoods are another essential feature. Most will be made of a weatherproof fabric, and some come equipped with fluffy genuine- or faux-fur trims that gently tickle your face with a touch of winter luxury. And then there are the pockets—no one wants to walk around in a blizzard with frozen fingers. (Look for fleece linings.) Finally, asses the length. Longer parkas offer more warmth and protection from the elements, while shorter ones are perfect for commuters who need to dodge frostbite without overheating on the subway.

While function is the defining characteristic of a good parka, a great one should also give your winter fits a serious upgrade. Pair it with a thermal and a chunky sweater for a no-brainer look, or go bold by layering it over a denim jacket, adding corduroys, and anchoring with sturdy boots.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6661. Past and Prologue: Burberry’s Daniel Lee is Bringing Fashion—and His Extended Family—Home.

Daniel Lee must be considering the notion of home a lot these days. Not just his 17th-century country house in his native Yorkshire, which he bought last year, but his London place, on a leafy 19th-century square, where he has lived for the last five years. Lee, Burberry’s chief creative officer, is enjoying a reprieve from having repair professionals in—the AC has been on the blink, the underfloor heating went awry, and he has already endured one soul-destroying flood. On this hot July morning, he has sequestered himself in the basement, decorated with a beige sectional sofa and a Gary Hume painting, Greenness Is a Kind of Grief. The room looks onto the garden, and Lee has taken to lying out on a lounger; by adjusting its angle and that of the television, he can watch soccer from outside.

“My social life is watching the match on TV; it’s a bit sad, isn’t it?” Lee says in a soft voice accented by dry humor. “I love all sport—Wimbledon’s great—but I prefer the energy of a football match to a tennis match. Tennis is very polite. People lose themselves at football—it’s like a cult, isn’t it?” I didn’t have Lee down as a sports fanatic, but he seems to revere footballers as much as the likes of Skepta and Olivia Colman, whom he loves collaborating with. (Lee supports Arsenal.) There’s also his daily 8 a.m. gym sessions before work. “The bench press is nice, because you can just lie there,” he says, laughing. “I don’t love cardio anymore—it hurts my knees.”

From left: Edie Campbell wears silk poplin trench coat and sequined georgette dress. Alva Claire wears map-print nylon sateen trench coat. Clothes and accessories (throughout), Burberry.

Lee, 40, tells me this as we sit in his garden, the first of our several meetings. In person, Lee is candid, funny, and thoughtful. “Daniel appreciates realness—and openness,” says Skepta. “And he has the best eye. I’d pretty much wear everything he makes.”

Appointed Burberry’s chief creative officer in 2022, Lee has taken the 170-year-old British brand from his highly conceptual debut, all electric-blue blanket checks and graphic red-rose prints, to his more recent collections, widely praised as much for their cool, considered functionality as for the cut and thrust of their forward direction. (Lee has also seen the brand reach pretax profits of over $65 million in 2026, up from an almost $88 million loss last year.) He came to Burberry after three years at Bottega Veneta—an era that flared up like a firework thanks to the success of the Cassette bag and Lido sandals, with Lee quitting before the spark extinguished itself. Before that: six years with Phoebe Philo at Celine, eventually becoming her design director; and before that Donna Karan in New York, following internships at Maison Margiela and Nicolas Ghesquière–era Balenciaga after his graduation from Central Saint Martins.

While the CV reads like a conceptualist designer’s dream, Lee’s Burberry role may be the most reflective of who he really is: pragmatic, unpretentious, driven by a sense of purpose. For his friend Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, who has known him since Bottega Veneta, Lee the person and the designer are one and the same. “The reason I feel so at ease in Daniel’s company is that he is grounded and down-to-earth,” she says. “He has this incredible talent and work ethic, yet there’s no pretense with him, no drama.”

From left: Romeo Beckham wears silk shirt, silk scarf, leather trousers, belt, and biker boots. Simone Ashley wears embellished satin dress, leather shoes, and frame bag. Paapa Essiedu wears nylon sateen trench coat, silk shirt, wool trousers, and leather shoes.

When he started at Burberry, Lee says, “it took me a minute to adjust. What I did in the past was about the dream [of fashion], and it was the accessories that were the focus. The clothes here are still the dream, yet they’re wearable and useful, not just for a show. Designing Burberry makes you question and consider everything.” He sees himself as “a making designer,” he says. “I enjoy being in the moment and working with instinct, with craft, with my hands—the physicality of that.”

Lee’s love of making comes from his family—his father Ian and mother Jenny, his brother Richard and sister Sophie. (Daniel is the eldest.) Ian was a mechanic before he retired, and he now lives in Lee’s Yorkshire home, which is not far from Bradford, where Lee was born and raised. He’s set up a workshop at the back of the house to renovate motorcycles, a lifelong passion, which delights his son to no end—when he and his brother were kids, they would ride the bikes in a field at the back of their house. His mom was the creative one. “She was always making—sewing curtains and baking fancy birthday cakes; she made a Noah’s ark for us, and she even made my aunt, who had a cleaning business, a vacuum cleaner,” Lee says. “It made me think, I just want a job where I can make things.”

Simone wears leather shirt, pleated leather skirt, boots, and bag.

Curtains that Lee’s mom sewed for the family living room now hang in one of the bedrooms at his house in Yorkshire, although “his” is a bit of a misnomer: Lee sees the place as his whole family’s home. The impetus to find somewhere in the area came in the aftermath of his mom’s death just before Christmas 2024. “In those moments,” Lee says, “the creative element of work was soothing—it was like therapy.” He hadn’t even been thinking about getting a place up north, but the undertow of emotion carried him there. His brother and sister-in-law, who live locally, were looking to buy a new home. Lee joined the hunt, and the house he ended up taking was the first and only one he saw. “Before that, I’d always had this quest to live abroad, work abroad, see the world,” he says. “When you’re young, you feel like you’ve got endless time—[then] you realize that, actually, time is finite. My family’s not going to be around forever. I want to spend more time with them.” (One area where Lee would rather keep his private life private is when it comes to dating, though he readily says that he’d like to start his own family: “I would love to have children.”)

His aunt Debbie, his mom’s sister, has moved next door to the 1680s house. It was Debbie who brought Lee to London for the first time when he was 12—they saw the London Eye, took in The Lion King, and ate at the then hip restaurant Sketch. “My aunt was being trendy,” Lee says, laughing affectionately. “She also took me to Harvey Nichols in Leeds. I wasn’t a kid growing up reading Vogue, but looking at the amazing windows at Harvey Nichols and seeing the clothes—that’s when I started to think about fashion.” His grandparents would take him to the Alhambra Theatre in Bradford to see the likes of Chicago (his grandmother’s favorite), which ignited a lifelong love of theater. (On a recent trip to New York, he caught the much-lauded revival of The Rocky Horror Show.)

While Lee’s family has always attended his Burberry runway shows, in the weeks and months after his mom’s death, the closeness deepened. His grandmother came to the show in February 2025 with a photograph of Lee’s mom in her handbag, and it was she who sat with him the night before the presentation as he worked on the last of the fittings. His sister, meanwhile, wore the Bur­berry trench that had been their mom’s. “She wore it to my first show,” Lee recalls.

“One thing about Daniel is that he has never forgotten his roots,” says Lee’s father, “and I think that’s why Yorkshire will always feel like home to him.” That feeling of reconnection is something to which Lee has given a lot of thought. “That’s the real value of the North [for me],” he says. “It gives you a sense of shared ownership of the difficult times, which makes things easier.”

Burberry’s headquarters are on Horseferry Road in London, walking distance from both Buckingham Palace and Tate Britain. Lee’s office and studio are on the seventh floor. He designs Tuesday to Thursday, reserving Monday and Friday for prep days—so the team, he says, can have their weekends free of work. Lee likes to be efficient—the late Virgil Abloh told him that creative directors shouldn’t waste their time emailing, so he doesn’t: He and his team speak constantly via WhatsApp instead.

In one corner of the vast workroom, Burberry archivist Carly Eck has assembled a rail of pieces taken from the 25,000 that the company holds—including the earliest trench, dating from 1917—with an eye to what Lee has responded to: the 1930s Highlander cape, with straps to allow freedom of movement; a motoring overall that Lee riffed on for his fall 2024 collection; and a coat worn by explorer Ernest Shackleton, which Lee also referenced in 2023. Eck and Lee get together at the beginning of every season to help build narratives connecting Burberry past and present. Lee’s intense curiosity has certainly paid unexpected dividends. The ridiculously cute duck hats that he included in his Burberry debut were inspired by drawings in one of the brand’s catalogs circa 1930s, laid out on a table nearby.

“What we do,” Lee says, “is try to provide people with answers about how to live the best possible way. We make clothes to protect people, to make them feel good, ready, sophisticated. I think the fashion is secondary. The design here starts from a place of utility, functionality, practicality—it has to work before it has to be, let’s say, decorative.” His Burberry collections thus far have variously offered blanket-lined parkas, battalion jackets, long kilts, jaunty capelets, and dandyish suiting; what model and equestrian Edie Campbell, who has worked with Burberry since she was 15 (“I still had braces!”), calls “very wearable, but with an edge. It’s joyful, and there’s a lightness and a playfulness to it.” Accessories—the ka-ching! successes for any fashion brand—are on his mind, even if a star hasn’t quite emerged yet.

But if the past is in the room, so is the future. Burberry’s spring 2027 collection, which he showed in September at Chelsea College of Arts—Jodie Turner-Smith, Jonathan Bailey, and Fiona Shaw on the front row; Central Cee on the catwalk—features trenches both diaphanous and etched with embroidery, as well as rendered in leather that’s been lavishly traced with beading; utilitarian cotton drill mixed with sequins; floral blousons and skirts worn with earthy, low-heeled buckled mules; and jewel-like high slingback shoes made a little less precious by being paired with slouchy socks. One thing always on Lee’s mind: making Burberry speak more to women. “The brand is born out of menswear, and the trenches are a very masculine thing,” he says. “We’re always trying to bring more femininity to it.”

Edie wears silk poplin jacket with shearling trim, sequined jersey dress, and leather shoes.

Color is one way into that, and it’s something that Lee has decisively brought to the brand from the very beginning with what he describes as softer, moorland tones; spring 2027, meanwhile, sings with shades of dusky pink, aubergine, duck-egg blue, and a soft-sunny yellow, reflecting the casual, lived-in feel that he wanted to impart on the clothes. Gary Hume, the painter, recalls meeting Lee when they began working on a Burberry project in 2024. Walking around Hume’s studio, they’d touch the art, communing with it. Having now worked with Lee, the artist feels that the designer’s use of color “doesn’t feel like it’s added on—it’s entirely integral to what Daniel does.”

For spring 2027, Lee also worked with the celebrated octogenarian print designer Celia Birtwell, an intrinsic part of the creative explosion in British art and design in the 1960s, along with her husband, designer Ossie Clark, and David Hockney, her close friend. Lee had gone to see the recent Hockney exhibition at the Serpentine Galleries in London—he feels a strong affinity with the Bradford-born artist, who died in June—and a gingham tablecloth that Hockney used as a leitmotif sparked an idea to collaborate with Birtwell, who created a check with a painterly feel to it and some rather charming vintage-wallpaper floral prints. They feel organic and fresh, a million miles away from CAD—or AI. “Celia brings a human hand, an emotional hand, to something,” Lee says, thrilled by what she has done. “We have an incredible archive, but sometimes it’s exciting to see new things.”

From left: Alva wears mohair/silk shawl coat and chevron-knit dress. Romeo wears leather jacket with shearling collar, silk shirt, flocked jeans, and belt.

Lee and I are to meet for the last time at the Regency Café near the Bur­berry headquarters. Founded in 1946, it hasn’t changed much since, still a haven of egg and chips, Formica, and tea so wonderfully strong you could stand a teaspoon up in it. In its own way, the café’s story isn’t so different from Burberry’s: halcyon Britain, yet a Britishness of global fascination. Seated among the Regency regulars are hordes of creatively dressed kids from all around the world Instagramming their full English breakfasts—the very kind of young, style-conscious types who Burberry would want to attract, though not only them, of course. It is an egalitarian brand, as much for the aristo in a beaten-up trench driving a Land Rover as it is for the bloke on the football terraces.

Pride in Britishness is, after all, intrinsic to Burberry. “It stands for heritage and culture, and all the things and all the people that those mean,” says model Alva Claire, and Lee seconds the thought. “We are the most famous British luxury brand,” he says, “but in a way we’re bigger than fashion: We are a British institution. We’re there to celebrate the best of Britain—great creativity and also great locations.” Lee recounts how so many of his Burberry shoots have been deliberately located outside of London—Skye, Somerset, Norfolk, the Lake District—and he readily agrees (while acknowledging the importance of London Fashion Week to Burberry) that it would be great to show somewhere else in the UK. But where? “Chanel did Manchester…,” I say; “Dior did Scotland,” he adds.

Lee on the winding, cobbled streets of Haworth, in West Yorkshire.

Right now, though, Lee is thinking about 170 years’ worth of moments. The anniversary is, he says, “always on our minds. How do we do it justice? We have been ambitious this year.” Indeed: As well as a monthslong campaign photographing 170 people all over the world wearing Burberry, a special exhibition, “The Burberry Trench: Crafting an Icon,” is at the V&A ahead of the company’s funding of the museum’s new costume wing, opening in 2028; another Burberry exhibition, “Ever Forward: The Archive On Stage,” opens this month in Shanghai.

Anyone would be asking themselves what’s left to do—and for Lee, there’s plenty. Top of mind for him, professionally, is transforming the brand’s retail environments for its 413 outposts around the world. Personally? Well, he wouldn’t mind, at some point in his life, living in a hot country. Yet he’s not in any rush. He wants progress to be measured and meaningful; to take it in stride. “I mean,” he says, smiling, “I really feel quite content.”

In this story: Hair, Mari Ohashi; makeup, Siobhan Furlong; grooming, Quelle Bester; manicurist, Robbie Tomkins; tailor, Della George.

#6660. These Cozy Shoes Are Too Chic to Keep Indoors

Slippers in public? These fashionable pairs make a convincing case.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

At this point, we’ve all probably accepted that slippers are no longer strictly house shoes. They’ve been part of our everyday wardrobes for years, and it’s hardly unusual to see someone wearing a fuzzy pair of slip-ons with jeans and a nice coat. What’s more interesting is how far brands have taken the idea lately. And honestly, some of these new styles are just really good shoes, slippers or not.

Take Ugg’s Western-inspired designs. Cowboy boots aren’t going anywhere, and the brand has found a way to bring that look into the comfortable footwear it’s known for. It’s a fun alternative to a traditional Western boot, especially if you want something a little more relaxed for everyday wear.

Brunch’s collaboration with Madhappy is another one worth knowing about. The two brands share co-founder Joshua Sitt, so the partnership makes sense, but the shoes themselves are what caught our attention. Made with colorful crochet and lined with shearling, they look like someone turned a chunky knit sweater into a slipper. And considering how much we love a good sweater this time of year, why shouldn’t our feet get a sweater of their own?

For Sitt, the idea of making slippers part of an everyday wardrobe has always been central to Brunch. “Originally, the entire concept for the brand was taking the hotel slipper product which is famously associated with vacation and travel, and bringing it into something you can wear every single day inside and outside of your home,” he tells ELLE.

You can see that thinking at work in the Madhappy collaboration. “The shoe itself morphs the comfort that both brands prioritize as well as the fashion pieces of both brands,” he says.

What’s particularly interesting is that this isn’t limited to brands you’d normally associate with slippers. Hunter, whose rain boots have been a wardrobe staple for years, has a cozy option of its own. Simkhai has entered the category, too, and Alo has a pair that feels especially fitting for the Pilates-to-coffee crowd. It’s a pretty good indication of just how much room there is to play with a shoe that used to be purely practical.

The styling is arguably the best part. A Western-inspired pair would look great with straight-leg jeans and a suede jacket, while a softer, more understated slipper can make tailored trousers and a wool coat feel less formal. You don’t need to rethink your wardrobe to wear them. In fact, that’s part of the appeal.

As Sitt points out, slippers haven’t exactly been the most considered purchase in our wardrobes. Ask people what pair they own, and “you’ll get some crickets,” he says. Or maybe they “stole a pair at a wedding.” No offense to wedding favors, but we think it’s time for an upgrade.

Whether you’re looking for an alternative to your usual boots or simply want a pair of slippers you won’t want to change out of before leaving the house, these are the styles worth a closer look. Shop our favorites below.
